El circuito de sintonía de una radio es: The tuning circuit of a radio is a band-pass RLC filter: the resonance sets the frequency it lets through, the quality factor Q narrows it and the Bode diagram shows how much it attenuates the neighbouring ones.
Se abre con el filtro «RLC paso banda» c: It opens with the "band-pass RLC" filter with L = 253.3 µH, C = 100 pF and R = 10 Ω, evaluated at 1009 kHz, the frequency of a station 9 kHz from the tuned one. We get f₀ = 1000 kHz and Q = 159 (the passband is f₀/Q = 6.28 kHz), and at 1009 kHz the signal is attenuated by about −9.6 dB.

En este momento, en el aire que te rodea: Right now, in the air around you there are dozens of radio stations, all at once, and your radio's antenna receives a little of each. Yet you only hear the one you choose.\n\nHow does the radio separate one from all the others? Each station uses **its own frequency**, like a different lane of the motorway. AM stations are about 9 kHz apart in the medium-wave band and FM ones, 200 kHz in their band. Turning the dial is choosing the lane.
es la antena de un cuarto de onda para 1: is the quarter-wave antenna for 1 MHz; for the 1 kHz sound 75 km would be needed.
Una antena emite bien si mide un cuarto: An antenna emits well if it is a quarter of the wavelength long, $λ = c/f$. For a 1 kHz sound, $λ = {3·10^8}/{10^3} = 300 "km"$: a 75 km antenna. Impossible.\n\nThe solution is to **mount the sound on a much faster wave**, the carrier. At 1 MHz the wavelength is $λ = 300 "m"$ and the 75 m antenna is already an ordinary tower. The carrier carries no information by itself: the sound is hidden in a small variation of it, and this is called modulating.

En la **amplitud modulada** la portadora:
In **amplitude modulation** the carrier keeps its frequency, but its amplitude rises and falls following the sound $m(t)$:

$s(t) = A [1 + 0.6 · m(t)] cos(ω_p t)$

The outline of the wave (the envelope, drawn dashed in the animation) is a copy of the sound. Since the sound has frequencies up to 4.5 kHz, the station occupies from $f_p − 4.5$ to $f_p + 4.5$ kHz, 9 kHz in total. That is why AM stations are 9 kHz apart. It is simple, but any noise (a storm, a motor) also changes the amplitude and is heard.
FM: cambia el ritmo de la onda: FM: changes the rhythm of the wave
es lo que se desvía la frecuencia de la: is how much the carrier frequency deviates with the loudest sound; each channel occupies 200 kHz.
En la **frecuencia modulada** la amplitu: In **frequency modulation** the amplitude never changes and it is the frequency that rises and falls: faster when the sound is positive and slower when it is negative. FM stations broadcast at about ${n(FM_MHZ)} MHz (wavelength $λ$ = ${n(datos.lamFM, 2)} m, antenna of about ${entero(datos.lamFM * 25)} cm) and deviate ±75 kHz.\n\nWith the amplitude fixed, the receiver can **clip** the height of the wave without losing the sound, and the noise, which gets in precisely in the amplitude, disappears. That is why FM sounds clean, and it also has room for more treble (up to 15 kHz) and for stereo. In return it takes more bandwidth, about 200 kHz per station, and only reaches as far as the horizon.

El dial de la radio mueve un condensador:
The radio dial moves a variable capacitor that, together with the antenna coil, forms a series RLC circuit. That circuit responds strongly to one frequency, the resonant one, and weakly to the others:

$f_0 = {1}/{2π√(L C)} = {1}/{2π√(${n(L * 1e6)}·10^{−6} · 10^{−10})} = ${entero(f0)} "kHz"$

Its quality factor is $Q = {ω_0 L}/R$ = ${entero(Q0)} (with R = 10 Ω of coil wire) and the bandwidth is $Δf = f_0/Q$ = **${n(BW0, 2)} kHz**. A neighbouring station at 9 kHz comes in with $|H|$ = ${n(g9, 2)} (${n(datos.g9dB)} dB): it is heard much less, but does not disappear. That is why modern radios also mix the signal with that of an oscillator down to a fixed frequency (455 kHz in AM, 10.7 MHz in FM) where much better filters can be used: this is the superheterodyne.

Ya sintonizada, la señal de AM sigue sie: Once tuned in, the AM signal is still the 1 MHz carrier with variable height: no loudspeaker could follow it. Only the envelope has to be kept.\n\nA **diode** lets only the positive half-cycles through and a **capacitor with a resistor** charges at each peak and discharges slowly between peaks. The constant $τ = R C = 10 "kΩ" · 2.2 "nF" = ${n(datos.tau * 1e6, 0)} "µs"$ acts as a low-pass filter: it follows the rise and fall of the envelope (200 µs for 5 kHz) but not the 1,000 cycles of the carrier per millisecond. What remains is the sound, which an amplifier takes to the loudspeaker. In FM the detector is different (a discriminator that converts each change in frequency into voltage), but the end is the same.
